newsitem.title: USA: Interest rate worries dampen U.S. auto sales outlook.
newsitem.headline: Interest rate worries dampen U.S. auto sales outlook.

text.p: U.S. vehicle sales blew past expectations in March, but automakers and analysts said Wednesday they were reluctant to raise full-year sales estimates because more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes may slow vehicle demand.
Industry sales in March ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 16.1 million total cars and trucks, the highest level in 15 months, which capped a stronger-than-expected first quarter.
"If that were to be sustained, we'd have additional interest rate increases, and that would tone the market down," Chrysler Corp. Chairman Robert Eaton said.
Chrysler, Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp. are not budging their sales forecasts, which contain a fair amount of wiggle room.

GM and Ford both estimate that U.S. vehicle sales, including medium and heavy trucks, will reach 15 million to 15.5 million units in 1997, while Chrysler's forecast calls for 15.2 million to 15.5 million units. Total U.S. vehicle sales in 1996 reached 15.4 million units.

"I think people don't want to get caught having to cut estimates later in the year," said Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi. "It's much less painful to be forced to raise estimates than to have to cut them."

As the market tries to anticipate the Fed's next move, many analysts are expecting at least another quarter of a percentage point increase in short-term interest rates in the near term, matching the Fed's action March 25.

David Littman, chief economist for Comerica Bank in Detroit, said that each half-point increase in interest rates would probably reduce U.S. vehicle sales by about 200,000 units, mainly by causing adjustable-rate mortgage payments and other financing costs to soak up more of buyers' disposable incomes.
There is usually a six-month lag before interest rate actions begin to affect car and truck sales, he said.
But automakers can be expected to fight back to some extent with higher incentives. Chrysler Tuesday offered a $595 national rebate for minivan models equipped with a left-side sliding door.
"As long as the Fed does no more than a half-point range of tightening, they can counter these moves at the retail level," Littman said.
Revisions to second-quarter production forecasts by the Big Three automakers this week indicate they have confidence in the near-term outlook.

GM left its second-quarter North American production unchanged at 1,550,000 vehicles, while Chrysler said Wednesday it boosted its second-quarter schedule by 9,200 cars and trucks to 809,000 vehicles.
Ford cut 10,000 cars out of its second-quarter production plans, but added 15,000 trucks, increasing its total to 1,207,000 vehicles from 1,202,000

But if the Fed raises rates by a full percentage point or more, it could cause significant reductions in demand, analysts said, particularly since the current recovery is in its seventh year. Automakers are already offering significant incentives and consumers are showing signs of being overextended.

"The consumer is punch drunk with credit," said Mike Robinet, an analyst with CSM Forecasting in Farmington Hills, Mich. "Banks and finance companies are pulling back on credit, and that's going to push your more marginal buyers out of the market."

Analyst George Magliano with WEFA Group in New York is one of the few analysts to increase his U.S. light vehicle sales forecast for the year, boosting it to about 14.9 million units from a bearish level of 14.7 million. The forecast excludes medium and heavy trucks, which typically run at about 300,000 vehicles per year.
However, Magliano cut his 1998 forecast to 14.7 million from 15.1 million, based partly on expectations that interest rate hikes will cool the economy significantly next year.
"I think it's taking a lot of incentive muscle to keep the market where it is," he said.
